newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia sends first war crimes suspect to Hague.
newsitem.headline: Croatia sends first war crimes suspect to Hague.

text.p: Croatia extradited its first war crimes suspect to the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague on Monday, days after the West tightened pressure on the country to comply with the court.

Zlatko Aleksovski, 36, was indicted for atrocities against Moslem civilians during the Bosnian war and was arrested in Croatia almost a year ago. However, the authorities had not sent him to the Hague, claiming he was ill.
One diplomat had said Croatia was under "serious pressure" to extradite Aleksovski, a Bosnian Croat, and the country's repeated promises to co-operate with The Hague had not been met.
Diplomats said doctors sent by the Tribunal examined Aleksovski last week and pronounced him fit to travel.
A government statement carried by the state news agency HINA said: "Legal conditions for Aleksovski's extradition have been met and...he was handed over to The Hague."
In Amsterdam the Tribunal said Aleksovski would make an initial public appearance before a panel of three judges at 1300 GMT on Tuesday to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty.
He is one of 15 Croats charged by the Tribunal with committing alleged atrocities against Moslems in the Lasva Valley region of central Bosnia in 1992 and 1993.
Aleksovski is accused of mistreating Moslem prisoners while commander of a detention camp at Kaonik, near Busovaca.

The indictment against him alleges that "many of the detainees under his control were subjected to inhumane treatment, including, but not limited to, excessive and cruel interrogation, physical and psychological harm, forced labour (digging trenches) in hazardous circumstances, being used as human shields and some were murdered or otherwise killed".

Last month the United States abstained from a vote by the International Monetary Fund to approve almost $500 million in loans to Croatia, as a sign of its dismay at Croatia's refusal to hand over suspects.
As the biggest and most influential donor to both the IMF and World Bank, U.S. lobbying could damage Croatia's ability to tap such institutions for capital to help rebuild its economy.
Diplomats have said if Washington opposes any multilateral loans it would also have to suspend bilateral assistance.

Assistance from elsewhere is relatively minimal, but the United States recently approved $28 million for reconstruction in eastern Croatia and granted around $20 million in other aid for post-war redevelopment in the country.

The tribunal, set up by the United Nations in 1993, has indicted more than 70 Serbs, Croats and Moslems for atrocities committed during the Bosnian conflict, but has been hampered by its inability to enforce the arrest of suspects still at large.

Aleksovski is the second Croat to be taken into tribunal custody following the voluntary surrender last year of General Tihomir Blaskic, a regional militia commander at the time of the alleged offences in central Bosnia.
Blaskic pleaded 'not guilty' in April 1996 but his trial has not yet started.
One senior diplomat told Reuters Croatia may not have wanted to hand Aleksovski over because of the refusal of other former Yugoslav republics to extradite their own suspects.
So far the Tribunal has only tried and sentenced one man to prison for war crimes committed during the 4-1/2 years of war that followed the break up of former Yugoslavia.
Drazen Erdemovic was sentenced in November to 10 years for taking part in executions in eastern Bosnia while serving with the Bosnian Serb army. He is an ethnic Croat.
